title: Forecasting Techniques & the 13-Week Cash Forecast (CMA P1-B · feeds P2-A)
lessonHtml:
Cold open — WIP is not cash

Real MBG context: MBG carries $14,480,000.00 of WIP and Riverton $11,360,000.00. Those assets do not pay payroll tomorrow. Cash depends on billing milestones, owner draws, retainage, collections, vendor terms, debt service, and project timing. The group also identified $400,000.00 stranded across seven dormant bank accounts, showing that total cash and usable cash can differ.

A 13-week cash forecast converts project and operating events into weekly receipts, disbursements, financing needs, and minimum cash. Its short horizon supports action while extending far enough to expose draw delays, payroll cycles, tax dates, and vendor peaks.

Forecast architecture

Begin with independently reconciled opening cash by entity and bank account. Then forecast cash receipts and disbursements by week:

Ending cash = Beginning cash + receipts − disbursements + financing inflows − financing repayments

Ending cash becomes the next week's beginning cash. Compare projected ending cash with required minimum cash to calculate borrowing or surplus. Do not include WIP, underbillings, or available credit as cash receipts until a supported timing event occurs.

Receipt drivers

  • Approved billing schedule and expected invoice submission.
  • Collection lag by owner/customer and historical behavior.
  • Construction draws tied to inspections or completion milestones.
  • Retainage releases only when contractual conditions are supportable.
  • Asset sales, tax refunds, equity, or debt based on approved evidence.

Disbursement drivers

  • Payroll through PayStream ACH or MBG check—never cash labor.
  • AP aging, vendor commitments, subcontract schedules, and retainage releases.
  • Taxes, insurance, debt service, equipment, and corporate overhead.
  • Intercompany transfers shown by both entities and eliminated only in a group cash bridge.

Worked 4-week slice

The following cash amounts are illustrative. MBG begins Week 1 with $500,000 and requires minimum cash of $250,000.

WeekBeginningReceiptsDisbursementsPre-financing endingBorrowing needed
1$500,000$300,000$450,000$350,000$0
2$350,000$200,000$400,000$150,000$100,000
3$250,000$600,000$300,000$550,000$0
4$550,000$150,000$500,000$200,000$50,000

After Week 2 borrowing, ending cash is $250,000 and becomes Week 3 beginning cash. If Week 4 also borrows $50,000, cumulative facility use is $150,000 before repayments. The forecast should show capacity, interest, covenant, approval, and availability rather than assuming borrowing is automatic.

Suppose Week 3's $600,000 receipt depends on a draw inspection that slips one week. Week 3 pre-financing ending becomes negative $50,000: $250,000 + $0 − $300,000. To preserve minimum cash, Week 3 requires $300,000 borrowing, not $0. Week 4 then receives the delayed $600,000 plus its planned $150,000, changing repayment capacity. Timing sensitivity matters more than quarterly totals.

Forecasting methods

Naive and moving-average methods extrapolate recent observations and work for stable recurring costs. A three-period moving average smooths noise but lags turning points. Exponential smoothing weights recent actuals more heavily; a higher smoothing constant reacts faster but increases volatility.

Regression estimates relationships such as labor hours driven by units installed. The equation Y = a + bX separates intercept and driver effect. Correlation does not prove causation; validate economic logic, residuals, stability, outliers, and relevant range.

Expected value probability-weights discrete outcomes. If an illustrative draw has 70% probability of $500,000 this week and 30% probability of $0, expected value is $350,000. For liquidity management, showing both scenarios may be safer than placing $350,000 in the cash column because no actual outcome pays $350,000.

Learning curves model declining cumulative average time as experience doubles. They fit repetitive work, not every custom construction task. Time-series decomposition separates trend, seasonality, cyclical, and irregular components; it requires enough consistent history.

Link WIP and draws without equating them

For each active job, forecast cost outflow, eligible progress, billing or draw trigger, submission date, approval lag, retainage, and collection date. Compare percentage complete, percentage billed, and percentage drawn. Divergence is a diagnostic, not automatically an error.

An underbilled job may signal an upcoming receipt opportunity or an unapproved/collectibility problem. An overbilled job may support current cash but creates future performance without equivalent billing. Cost-to-complete increases can raise future cash need while reducing margin. Update both the WIP forecast and cash forecast from the same operational facts.

Use the real WIP balances as reconciliation anchors, not as forecast receipts. MBG and Riverton forecasts remain separate because bank and funding access are entity-specific. A group view shows intercompany transfers twice at entity level—outflow and inflow—then eliminates them from group net cash movement.

Rolling forecast governance

Every week, replace forecast with actual, explain variance, and add a new week so the horizon remains 13 weeks. Lock prior versions. Track forecast accuracy by category and horizon: Week 1 should generally be more accurate than Week 13. Separate timing variance from amount variance.

Assign owners: project teams own milestone evidence; AP owns payment schedules; payroll owns payroll dates; treasury owns bank and financing; finance integrates and challenges. Maintain a source and confidence rating for material receipts. Do not let a favorable plug restore minimum cash.

Base, downside, and severe-but-plausible scenarios should specify triggers and actions. A downside case can delay major draws, accelerate material purchases, or reduce available credit. Avoid double-counting correlated risks.

Accuracy measurement and backtesting

Forecast error should be measured consistently. For a cash category, error can be actual minus forecast; absolute error removes favorable/unfavorable direction; percentage error scales for size but becomes unstable near zero. Mean absolute error is easy to explain, while mean absolute percentage error can overemphasize small denominators. Bias is the signed average error and reveals systematic optimism or conservatism.

Assume illustrative weekly receipts were forecast at $400,000, $500,000, and $300,000, while actuals were $350,000, $650,000, and $250,000. Signed errors actual minus forecast are negative $50,000, positive $150,000, and negative $50,000. Mean signed error is positive $16,666.67, while mean absolute error is $83,333.33. The positive bias is not proof of accuracy; large offsetting errors can produce a small average.

Backtesting asks whether assumptions performed as expected and why. Classify misses as timing, amount, scope, source-data, or judgment. Repeated owner-payment delays should change the collection-lag assumption. A one-time storm may remain a scenario risk rather than a new base trend. Record forecast changes prospectively; do not rewrite archived versions.

Use confidence tiers for receipts: committed and confirmed, probable with evidence, and scenario-only. Apply stronger challenge to large, late-horizon, or externally dependent receipts. Forecast governance should prohibit using unsupported intercompany transfers or new debt merely to eliminate a projected deficit.

Regression discipline

Before using a regression, plot the data, inspect sample size and outliers, test whether the relationship makes operational sense, and avoid extrapolating outside the observed range. Structural changes—new labor process, entity, or pricing—can make historical coefficients obsolete. Forecasting is a controlled learning process, not permanent trust in one equation.

CMA Part 2 Crossover — Financial Statement Analysis

Cash forecasting supports liquidity analysis, working capital, financing decisions, and risk management. Part 2 questions connect timing assumptions to borrowing needs, interest, covenant headroom, and value. A profitable project can still create a liquidity crisis.

Practice and recap

  1. Start with bank-reconciled cash by entity.
  2. Forecast receipts from dated, supported milestones and collection lags.
  3. Forecast disbursements from payroll, AP, commitments, tax, and debt schedules.
  4. Calculate minimum-cash funding needs weekly.
  5. Run draw-delay and cost-overrun scenarios.
  6. Roll actuals, preserve versions, and measure accuracy.

Recap: a 13-week forecast is an operating control, not a spreadsheet prediction. It connects WIP events to cash timing, exposes funding needs early, and forces assumptions to have owners and evidence.

flashcards.front: What is the weekly cash formula?
flashcards.back: Beginning cash + receipts − disbursements + financing inflows − financing repayments = ending cash.

flashcards.front: Why is WIP not a cash receipt?
flashcards.back: WIP represents accumulated project cost; cash requires billing/draw, approval, and collection events.

flashcards.front: What real cash was stranded in dormant accounts?
What does a rolling 13-week forecast do?
flashcards.back: Replaces elapsed forecast with actual and adds a new week to keep a constant horizon.
The probability-weighted average of possible outcomes.

flashcards.front: Why distinguish timing and amount variance?
flashcards.back: A correct amount in the wrong week has different liquidity implications from a wrong amount.

flashcards.front: What happens to intercompany transfers in a group cash view?
flashcards.back: Show both entity flows, then eliminate the internal group movement.

flashcards.front: Which MBG labor payments are permitted?
flashcards.back: PayStream ACH or MBG check; never cash labor.

questions.q: Illustrative beginning cash is $350,000, receipts $200,000, and disbursements $400,000. Pre-financing ending cash is:
If required minimum cash is $250,000, borrowing needed in that week is:
A $500,000 draw has 70% chance this week and 30% chance of zero. Expected value is:
Why might scenario presentation be better than booking the $350,000 expected value in cash?
choices: Neither actual outcome equals $350,000 and liquidity needs are nonlinear
questions.explain: The business receives either $500,000 or $0, so each scenario's funding need matters.

questions.q: Which method generally lags turning points because it smooths recent periods?
questions.explain: Moving averages damp noise but respond slowly to a change in direction.

questions.q: What should anchor opening forecast cash?
questions.explain: Opening cash must tie to independent bank evidence and the ledger reconciliation.

questions.q: A profitable project causes a near-term cash deficit. Which conclusion is correct?
choices: Profit and cash timing are distinct
WIP should be treated as cash
questions.explain: Accrual profit can precede collection while payroll and vendors require cash.
